# SK1034 — Use the `Count` property, not `Count()` or `Any()`

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`list.Count() > 0` and `list.Any()` on something that already has a `Count`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 0.6 |
| ReSharper | `UseCollectionCountProperty` (`resharper_use_collection_count_property_highlighting`) |

## Why

`Enumerable.Count()` has a fast path for `ICollection` and `Any()` allocates an enumerator; both are strictly more work than reading the property, and both hide from the reader that the length is already known. The value is legibility more than speed.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (items.Any()) {
    Consume(items);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
if (items.Count > 0) {
    Consume(items);
}
```

## The ReSharper mapping

Three inspections cover this ground: use_collection_count_property, replace_with_single_call_to_any and replace_with_single_call_to_count, all `suggestion` in the export. The first is recorded; the mapping is many-to-one from ReSharper's side. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

## When it does not fire

Only fires when the invoked method is exactly `System.Linq.Enumerable.Count()` or `Enumerable.Any()` with no argument, the receiver's type has an accessible instance `Count` (or `Length`) property of type `int`, and the receiver expression is a plain identifier or member-access chain with no invocation in it — so `GetItems().Any()` is left alone, because reading `.Count` on it would still call `GetItems()` and the rewrite is only obviously equivalent when the receiver is a variable. Silent on `IQueryable`, where `Any()` is a database round-trip and `Count` is not the same query.
